title: Revelation, the Prophet and the Pillars
bigQuestion: How do the Qur'an and the Five Pillars shape a Muslim's day, year and life, and what do they tell an outside student about what Islam values?

story.title: Ramadan in Room 214
story.kicker: For one month each year, a Chicago high school runs on two clocks at once: the bell schedule, and the sun.
paragraphs: It is the second week of Ramadan, and the lunchroom at a high school on Chicago's Northwest Side is louder than usual, because about thirty students are not in it. They are in Room 214, a science lab that a teacher opened at lunch so that fasting students would have somewhere to sit that did not smell like pizza. Some are doing homework. Two are asleep with their heads on their arms. A junior named Amina is explaining to a friend who is not Muslim why she woke up at 4:15 that morning to eat.

The friend has questions, and Amina does not mind them. No, not even water, from the first light before dawn until the sun goes down. Yes, every day for about a month. No, not little kids, not people who are sick, not travelers, not women who are pregnant or nursing; the Qur'an itself lists exceptions. The point, she says, is not to suffer. The point is to feel what hunger is, to remember people who feel it every day, and to spend a month paying closer attention to God.

The gym teacher has quietly stopped requiring the mile run during Ramadan. The lunch ladies, who saw the empty tables the first day, now pack extra fruit into bags that the fasting students take home for later. At 7:40 in the evening, in a dozen kitchens across the neighborhood, the same thing happens: someone checks a phone app or a printed schedule, hears the call to sunset prayer, and breaks the fast with a date and a glass of water, the way Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad did.

On the last Friday of the month, the school's Muslim Student Association hosts an iftar, the evening meal that ends the fast, in the cafeteria. Two hundred people come, including the principal, the gym teacher and Amina's friend. Before anyone eats, a senior stands and recites a few verses of the Qur'an in Arabic, in a slow, rising chant. Almost no one in the room speaks Arabic, but everyone is quiet. Then the trays come out, and it is, after all, a high school cafeteria.

A month like this is a good place to start studying Islam, because so much of the tradition is visible in it: a text recited aloud, a practice timed by the sun, a community that eats together, and a set of rules that bend for the sick and the young. This chapter follows those threads back to their sources: the Arabia of the seventh century, the man Muslims call the Prophet, the book they call the Qur'an, and the five practices, the pillars, that hold the whole structure up.
story.think: Amina's school changed several small things during Ramadan. What does a public school have to balance when students practice a religion during the school day?

lessons.title: Arabia Before Islam
lessons.mainIdea: Seventh-century Arabia was a land of trading towns and tribes, with many gods, a famous shrine at Mecca, and neighbors who were Jewish and Christian.
reading: Picture Mecca around the year 600. It sits in a dry valley in western Arabia, on a caravan route that carries spices, leather and cloth between Yemen in the south and Syria in the north. In the middle of town stands a cube-shaped stone building called the *Kaaba*. Arabs from across the peninsula travel to it each year, and during the pilgrimage months fighting stops so that they can come safely. Inside and around the Kaaba, historians say, stood images of many tribal gods.

Most Arabs at this time were organized by *tribe*, a large group of related families that protected its members and avenged them when they were wronged. There was no king and no central government. Loyalty, generosity and courage were prized; poetry was the great art, recited from memory at fairs and markets. Muslims later called this period the *jahiliyya*, a word usually translated as the age of ignorance, meaning the time before the Qur'an's guidance arrived.

Arabia was not cut off from the wider world. Jewish tribes had lived in the oasis town of Yathrib, later called Medina, for centuries. Christian communities existed in Yemen, in the north near Syria and among some Arab tribes. The two great empires of the day, the Christian Byzantine Empire and the Zoroastrian Persian Empire, fought long wars just beyond Arabia's borders. Stories of Abraham, Moses and Jesus were known in Mecca before Islam began.

Islamic tradition also remembers a few Meccans called *hanifs* who rejected the tribal gods and worshiped one God without belonging to a Jewish or Christian community. Muslims believe that the Kaaba itself was first built by Abraham and his son Ishmael as a house for the one God, and that Meccans had forgotten this over time. Whether or not a student accepts that account, it explains why the Kaaba matters so much in the rest of this story.

words.d: the cube-shaped stone shrine in Mecca that Muslims face in prayer and circle during the hajj
a large group of related families in pre-Islamic Arabia that protected and avenged its members
the Muslim term for Arabia before Islam, usually translated as the age of ignorance
in Islamic tradition, Arabs before Muhammad who worshiped one God without being Jewish or Christian

look.title: A Town on a Trade Route
look.text: Mecca had little farmland and no river. It grew rich anyway, because caravans stopped there and because pilgrims came to the Kaaba every year. The tribe that controlled the shrine, the Quraysh, also controlled the trade. Now imagine a preacher from that same tribe who says the images at the shrine are false gods.
look.prompt: Why might Mecca's leading families have seen such a message as a threat to their money and power, not only to their religion?

A library of Arabic poetry

The period in Arabia before the Qur'an, often translated as the age of ignorance
The trade route between Yemen and Syria

check.why: Jahiliyya is the Muslim name for pre-Islamic Arabia, the time before the guidance of the Qur'an.

Arabia was ruled by one central government

Everyone in Arabia already worshiped one God
check.why: Jews and Christians lived in and around Arabia, so biblical stories were known in Mecca. Arabia had no central government.

lessons.title: The First Revelation
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that in about 610 the angel Gabriel brought Muhammad the first words of the Qur'an in a cave near Mecca, beginning twenty-three years of revelation.
reading: Islamic tradition tells the story this way. *Muhammad* was born in Mecca around 570 into the Quraysh tribe. His father died before his birth and his mother when he was about six, so he was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle, Abu Talib. He worked in the caravan trade and earned a reputation for honesty; people called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. At about twenty-five he married Khadija, a wealthy merchant widow who employed him, and they had several children.

Muhammad had a habit of going alone to a cave on Mount Hira, outside Mecca, to think and pray. Muslims believe that one night in about 610, when he was about forty, the angel *Gabriel* (Jibril in Arabic) appeared to him and commanded, Recite. Muhammad answered that he could not recite. The command came again, and then the first words of what became the Qur'an: verses that speak of a Lord who created humans and taught them by the pen. Muslims call this night Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power.

According to the tradition, Muhammad came home shaking and asked Khadija to cover him. She comforted him, and she became the first person to believe that the message was from God. Over the next twenty-three years, Muslims hold, Gabriel brought further *revelation* in pieces, sometimes a few verses at a time, until Muhammad's death in 632. Muhammad recited each passage to his followers, who memorized it and wrote parts down on whatever was at hand.

Muslims do not believe that Muhammad wrote the Qur'an or that he was divine. They believe he was a *prophet*, a human messenger chosen to deliver God's words, in the same line as Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that he was the last of them. That is why Muslims often add the words peace be upon him after his name, and why a student of religion writes Muslims believe when describing these events, rather than stating them as settled history.

words.d: the man Muslims believe was God's final prophet; born in Mecca c. 570, died in Medina in 632
the angel (Jibril in Arabic) who Muslims believe brought the Qur'an to Muhammad
a message that believers hold was sent by God; for Muslims, the words of the Qur'an
a human messenger chosen by God; Muslims count Muhammad as the last in a line that includes Moses and Jesus

look.title: The First Words

look.prompt: The first thing this passage commands is to recite, and it praises a God who teaches by the pen. What does that suggest about how the tradition would come to value reading, memory and learning?

check.why: Tradition places the first revelation in the cave on Mount Hira outside Mecca, in about 610, when Muhammad was about forty.

check.why: Muslims believe Muhammad was a human messenger who recited what Gabriel brought from God; they do not consider him the author or divine.

lessons.title: Mecca, Medina and the Hijra
lessons.mainIdea: Rejected in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers moved to Medina in 622, the hijra that starts the Muslim calendar, and built the first Muslim community there.
reading: For about a dozen years Muhammad preached in Mecca. His message, that there is one God, that the idols at the Kaaba are false, that the rich must care for the poor and that everyone will be judged, won a small following: family members, some young people, some enslaved people and poor Meccans. Mecca's leading families opposed him. The shrine and its pilgrims were their business, and a preacher attacking the tribal gods threatened both their beliefs and their income. Some early Muslims were beaten; a few were killed.

In 622, after Khadija and Abu Talib had died and the danger had grown, Muhammad accepted an invitation from the town of Yathrib, about 200 miles north, where feuding tribes wanted an outside judge. He and his followers moved there in small groups. This move is the *hijra*, meaning migration. It matters so much that the Islamic calendar counts years from it: the year 622 CE is year 1 AH, from the Latin for in the year of the hijra. Yathrib became known as Medina, from Madinat al-Nabi, the city of the Prophet.

In *Medina* Muhammad was no longer only a preacher but the leader of a community, the *umma*, the body of all Muslims. He built the first mosque, set up rules for how Muslims, Jews and others in the town would live together, and led the community through several battles with Mecca, including Badr in 624 and Uhud in 625. The revelations from these years, Muslims note, deal more often with law, family and community than the shorter, urgent Meccan passages.

In 630 Muhammad returned to Mecca at the head of a large force, and the city surrendered with little fighting. According to tradition he cleared the Kaaba of its idols and rededicated it to the one God, while granting a general pardon to most of his former enemies. He died in Medina in 632 and is buried there. By then most of Arabia's tribes had accepted Islam. The question of who would lead the umma after him is taken up in the next chapter.

words.d: the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622; year 1 of the Islamic calendar
the city north of Mecca (formerly Yathrib) where Muhammad led the first Muslim community and is buried
the worldwide community of Muslims

check.why: The hijra of 622 marks the founding of the first Muslim community, so Muslims count years from it (AH).

choices: The first mosque in Medina

check.why: The umma is the worldwide body of Muslims, which took shape as a community in Medina.

choices: It attacked the tribal gods and threatened the income the shrine and pilgrims brought them
He wanted to move the Kaaba to Medina

check.why: The Quraysh controlled the Kaaba and its pilgrim trade; a message against the idols threatened both their beliefs and their business.

lessons.title: How the Qur'an Is Arranged
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an has 114 suras arranged roughly from longest to shortest, not in the order revealed, and Muslims believe its Arabic text is God's own speech.
reading: Open a printed Qur'an and the first thing you meet is not the first revelation from Mount Hira. It is a short prayer of seven verses called al-Fatiha, the Opening. After it comes the longest chapter in the book, and the chapters then generally grow shorter until the last ones are only a few lines. Each chapter is a *sura*, and each verse is an *ayah*, a word that also means a sign. There are 114 suras and, by the usual count, 6,236 ayahs.

The order is not chronological. Muslims believe the passages were revealed over twenty-three years, and scholars sort suras into *Meccan* ones, usually short and intense, warning of judgment and calling people to the one God, and *Medinan* ones, usually longer, with laws about marriage, inheritance, contracts and the community. A single sura can contain verses from both periods. Each sura has a name taken from a word in it: the Cow, the Bee, the Light, the Night.

For daily reading, the Qur'an is also divided into thirty roughly equal parts called *juz'*. A person who reads one juz' each night finishes the whole book in a month, which is exactly what many Muslims do during Ramadan. Muslims believe the text was fixed in writing under the third caliph, Uthman, in the 650s, when official copies were sent to the main cities. The Arabic text used today is, Muslims hold, unchanged since then.

Two features surprise students who expect a book like the Bible. First, the Qur'an is mostly not a narrative; it speaks directly, often as God addressing the listener, and returns again and again to the same themes. Second, it assumes you already know the stories of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses and Jesus, and refers to them briefly to make a point. The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians People of the Book, communities that also received scriptures.

words.d: a chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114, arranged roughly from longest to shortest
a verse of the Qur'an; the word also means a sign
suras Muslims and scholars date to Muhammad's years in Mecca; usually short and focused on God and judgment
suras dated to the years in Medina; usually longer, with more law and community rules
one of thirty roughly equal parts of the Qur'an, used for reading it through in a month

check.why: An ayah is a verse; a sura is a chapter; a juz' is a reading portion; al-Fatiha is the opening.

lessons.title: Recitation and Translation
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims experience the Qur'an first as sound recited in Arabic; translations are considered interpretations of its meaning, not the Qur'an itself.
reading: The word *Qur'an* means recitation. Before it was a book it was a sound, and for most Muslims it still is. Children learn to recite suras long before they can read them, and a person who has memorized the whole text is honored with the title *hafiz*, meaning guardian. There are set styles of melodic recitation called tajwid, with rules for how long each vowel is held and where to breathe. Famous reciters have followings the way singers do, and recitation contests draw thousands of listeners.

This is why the Arabic matters so much. Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's speech in the very words revealed to Muhammad, so the Arabic text is the Qur'an and a translation is not. An English version is usually titled something like The Meaning of the Glorious Qur'an to make this point. Muslims who do not speak Arabic, and that is most of the world's Muslims, still pray in Arabic and often study the original alongside a translation in their own language.

For a student in a public school, translations are what we have, and it helps to know a little about them. The first English versions were made by non-Muslims, and some were hostile. J. M. Rodwell's translation (1861) and E. H. Palmer's (1880) are now in the public domain and were used by scholars for decades. Twentieth-century translations by Muslims, such as Marmaduke Pickthall's (1930) and Abdullah Yusuf Ali's (1934), are widely read today, along with many newer versions. Rodwell even rearranged the suras into what he thought was their historical order.

Comparing two translations of one verse is a good habit for this course, as unit 1 taught. A single Arabic word may be rendered God or Allah, the Merciful or the Compassionate, recite or read. None of these choices is neutral. When this course quotes the Qur'an in paraphrase, it is offering one careful reading of the meaning, and a Muslim reader would remind you that the real thing is the Arabic.

words.d: the sacred book of Islam, which Muslims believe is God's speech revealed to Muhammad; the word means recitation
a person who has memorized the entire Qur'an; the word means guardian
the rules and art of reciting the Qur'an correctly and melodically

lessons.title: Tawhid: The Oneness of God
lessons.mainIdea: Tawhid, the absolute oneness of God, is the center of Islamic belief, and it shapes what Muslims say about prophets, scripture, angels and judgment.
reading: Sura 112 is one of the shortest chapters in the Qur'an, four lines that many Muslims recite every day. It says that God is one, eternal and absolute, that God does not beget and was not begotten, and that nothing is like God. Muslims call the teaching packed into those lines *tawhid*, the oneness of God. It is the first half of the Muslim declaration of faith, and everything else in Islam is meant to follow from it.

The opposite of tawhid is *shirk*, associating anything else with God: worshiping idols, as Meccans did before Islam, but also treating wealth, power or any person as if it were divine. The Qur'an treats shirk as the gravest error. This is also why Muslims do not accept the Christian teaching that Jesus is the Son of God or part of a Trinity, even though the Qur'an honors Jesus as a prophet born of the Virgin Mary who worked miracles. Muslims and Christians agree on much about Jesus and differ here.

From tawhid flow the other core beliefs that Muslim teachers list. Muslims believe in angels, God's messengers, including Gabriel. They believe God sent scriptures before the Qur'an, the Torah to Moses, the Psalms to David, the Gospel to Jesus, but that those texts were altered over time, which the Qur'an corrects. They believe in a line of prophets ending with Muhammad. And they believe in a Day of Judgment, when each person is raised and answers for their deeds, followed by paradise or hell.

Muslims speak of God with ninety-nine names drawn from the Qur'an: the Merciful, the Compassionate, the Just, the Forgiving, the Creator, the Light. You may see them on prayer beads or on the walls of a mosque. The word *Allah* is simply Arabic for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use it too. Understanding tawhid explains a great deal about Muslim practice, from the ban on images in worship to the fact that prayer is addressed to God alone.

words.d: the Islamic teaching that God is absolutely one, with no partners, equals or offspring
associating anything or anyone with God; in Islam, the gravest error
the Arabic word for God, used by Arabic-speaking Muslims, Christians and Jews
in Islamic belief, the day when all people are raised and judged by God for their deeds

lessons.title: Shahada and Salat
lessons.mainIdea: The first two pillars are the declaration of faith, which makes a person a Muslim, and the five daily prayers that structure every day.
reading: Muslim teachers sum up the practice of Islam in five duties called the *Five Pillars*, an image of posts holding up a roof. A well-known hadith, a report of the Prophet's words, lists them: testimony of faith, prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan and pilgrimage. The first is the *shahada*, the declaration: There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Saying it sincerely, in Arabic, before witnesses, is how a person becomes a Muslim. It is whispered into a newborn's ear and, if possible, is the last thing a dying person says.

The second pillar is *salat*, ritual prayer five times a day: before sunrise, at midday, in the afternoon, just after sunset and at night. The times shift with the sun, so they change through the year; in a Chicago June the last prayer falls after 10 p.m. Before praying, a Muslim performs *wudu*, washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head and feet. Then, facing the *qibla*, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, the worshiper recites al-Fatiha and other verses while standing, bowing, prostrating with the forehead on the ground and sitting, in a set sequence.

Salat can be done anywhere clean, on a mat at home, in an office, in an airport, but praying together is preferred, and the midday prayer on Friday, jumu'ah, is a congregational prayer at the mosque with a sermon. The call to prayer, the adhan, is chanted from the mosque in Arabic and begins Allahu akbar, God is greater. In Muslim-majority countries it sounds from loudspeakers five times a day; in Chicago it is more often an app notification.

Notice what these two pillars do. The shahada names the two things a Muslim must affirm, one God and one final messenger, and nothing more; there is no long creed to sign. Salat then takes that belief and puts it into the body five times a day, at the same times and in the same direction as more than a billion other people. Muslims often describe salat as a conversation with God and as a reset that pulls them out of ordinary business.

words.d: the five core practices of Islam: shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj
the Muslim declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God
the ritual prayer Muslims perform five times a day facing Mecca
the washing of hands, face, arms, head and feet before prayer
the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca, which Muslims face when they pray

lessons.title: Zakat and the Ramadan Fast
lessons.mainIdea: Zakat, a yearly share of wealth given to those in need, and sawm, the dawn-to-sunset fast of Ramadan, turn belief into discipline and care for others.
reading: The third pillar is *zakat*, which means purification. Once a year, Muslims who have savings above a set minimum give a fixed share, traditionally 2.5 percent of that wealth, to people in need. The Qur'an names who may receive it: the poor, the needy, those in debt, travelers, those who collect it and others. Zakat is not the same as ordinary charity, which Muslims call sadaqa and give freely; zakat is a duty, and in some countries it is collected like a tax. Many Muslims calculate it during Ramadan.

The fourth pillar is *sawm*, fasting during *Ramadan*, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, the month in which Muslims believe the Qur'an was first revealed. From the first light before dawn until sunset, adults do not eat, drink, smoke or have sexual relations. The Qur'an lists exceptions: the sick, travelers, and by extension pregnant and nursing women and the elderly, who make up the days later or feed the poor instead. Children are not required to fast, though many start with partial days.

Because the Islamic calendar follows the moon, its year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan moves earlier each year and circles through all the seasons in about thirty-three years. A Chicago Ramadan in December means a fast of about nine and a half hours; one in June means about sixteen and a half. Each day ends with the *iftar*, the fast-breaking meal, often begun with dates and water. The pre-dawn meal is called suhoor.

Muslims describe Ramadan as much more than not eating. Mosques are full for extra night prayers, during which the whole Qur'an is recited over the month. People try to give up gossip and anger, read more, and give more. The last ten nights include Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, when Muslims believe the first revelation came and prayer is said to be especially valuable. The month ends with a festival, Eid al-Fitr, which the next section describes.

words.d: the yearly duty to give a set share of one's wealth, traditionally 2.5 percent of savings, to those in need
fasting; the pillar of fasting from dawn to sunset during Ramadan
the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, when Muslims fast and remember the first revelation of the Qur'an
the meal that breaks the fast at sunset during Ramadan

look.title: The Qur'an on the Fast
look.text: Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for people. Whoever of you is present in the month should fast in it. But whoever is sick or on a journey should fast the same number of other days. God wants ease for you, not hardship.
look.cite: Qur'an, Sura 2 (al-Baqara), verse 185, in a plain paraphrase
look.prompt: The verse gives the rule and the exceptions in the same breath. What does the phrase about ease, not hardship, suggest about how Muslims are meant to read the rest of the rules?

check.q: How does zakat differ from ordinary charity in Islam?
choices: Zakat is given only to mosques
Zakat is a required yearly share of wealth, while sadaqa is voluntary giving
Zakat is given only during the hajj
Zakat is a fast, not a gift
check.why: Zakat is a duty, a fixed share of savings given each year; sadaqa is charity given freely.

check.q: Why does Ramadan fall at a different time of the solar year each year?
choices: Each country chooses its own Ramadan dates
It always falls in the hottest month
The Islamic calendar follows the moon and is about eleven days shorter than the solar year
It is fixed to the spring equinox
check.why: The lunar Islamic year is shorter, so Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year and cycles through the seasons.

check.q: According to the Qur'an, who is excused from fasting during Ramadan?
choices: Only children under five
No one; every Muslim must fast
Anyone who finds it difficult
The sick and travelers, who make up the days later
check.why: Sura 2:185 excuses the sick and travelers and asks them to fast the same number of days later; the tradition extends this to others.

lessons.title: The Hajj
lessons.mainIdea: The hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca required once in a lifetime for those who are able, gathers millions of Muslims to retrace the steps of Abraham, Hagar and Muhammad.
reading: The fifth pillar is the *hajj*, the pilgrimage to Mecca during the last month of the Islamic calendar, Dhu al-Hijjah. Every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able is expected to make it once in a lifetime. In recent years about two million pilgrims have come each year from nearly every country on earth; Saudi Arabia limits numbers through a quota system because the holy sites cannot hold more. Non-Muslims are not permitted to enter Mecca, so what outsiders know comes from pilgrims' accounts and films.

Before arriving, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity called *ihram*. Men put on two plain white unsewn cloths; women wear simple modest dress, often white. A king and a janitor look the same, which is the point. Pilgrims then perform *tawaf*, walking seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, and walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa. Muslims believe this retraces the steps of Hagar, Abraham's wife, as she searched for water for her son Ishmael, until the spring of Zamzam appeared.

The heart of the hajj is the day of standing at the plain of Arafat, a few miles outside Mecca, where pilgrims spend the afternoon in prayer. Muslims believe the Prophet gave his farewell sermon there in 632. Pilgrims then camp at Muzdalifa, throw pebbles at three stone pillars at Mina, which represents Abraham rejecting temptation, and sacrifice an animal, recalling Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son. Muslims around the world celebrate that day as Eid al-Adha.

People who have completed the hajj may add the title hajji or hajja to their name. Many describe it as the most important experience of their lives. The American Muslim leader Malcolm X, after his 1964 hajj, wrote that praying beside pilgrims of every color changed his views about race. A shorter visit to Mecca at any other time of year, the umra, is encouraged but does not fulfill the pillar.

words.d: the pilgrimage to Mecca in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, required once in a lifetime for Muslims who are able
the state of ritual purity for pilgrimage, marked by plain white garments for men and simple dress for women
walking seven times around the Kaaba during pilgrimage
the plain outside Mecca where pilgrims stand in prayer on the central day of the hajj

look.title: Dressed the Same
look.text: A pilgrim from Indonesia, a pilgrim from Nigeria and a pilgrim from suburban Chicago stand side by side at Arafat. All three men wear two plain white cloths. No one can tell from looking who is a surgeon, who drives a truck, or who saved for twenty years to be there.
look.prompt: What is the ihram dress code teaching, and how does it connect to the belief in tawhid and the Day of Judgment from earlier in this chapter?

check.q: Who is required to perform the hajj?
choices: Every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able, once in a lifetime
Every Muslim, every year
Only Muslims born in Saudi Arabia
Only men over fifty
check.why: The hajj is required once in a lifetime for adult Muslims who have the health and means to make it.

check.q: What do Muslims believe the walk between Safa and Marwa retraces?
choices: Muhammad's journey from Mecca to Medina
Hagar's search for water for her son Ishmael
The route of the first caravan to Syria
The path of the angel Gabriel to Mount Hira
check.why: Muslims believe Hagar ran between the two hills searching for water until the spring of Zamzam appeared.

check.q: What does the sacrifice at the end of the hajj recall?
choices: The Battle of Badr
The building of the first mosque in Medina
Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son
The revelation of Sura 96
check.why: The sacrifice at Mina, celebrated worldwide as Eid al-Adha, recalls Abraham's readiness to obey God by sacrificing his son.

lessons.title: The Two Eids
lessons.mainIdea: Islam has two major festivals: Eid al-Fitr, which ends Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha, which marks the sacrifice of the hajj; both center on prayer, giving and shared meals.
reading: The word *Eid* means festival, and Muslims celebrate two each year. *Eid al-Fitr*, the festival of breaking the fast, begins when the new moon is sighted at the end of Ramadan. Before the holiday prayer, each family gives a small food or cash donation, zakat al-fitr, so that poor families can celebrate too. Then large crowds gather early in the morning for a special prayer, often outdoors or in a rented hall because no mosque is big enough. In the Chicago area, Eid prayers have filled convention halls and stadium fields.

After the prayer comes visiting: new clothes, sweets, gifts of money to children, and a long day of meals with relatives and friends. Greetings of Eid Mubarak, blessed festival, are exchanged. Because Ramadan is a month of discipline, Muslims often describe the morning of Eid, when they may eat in daylight again, as a feeling of relief and gratitude. In many families the first breakfast in a month is a small ceremony.

*Eid al-Adha*, the festival of sacrifice, falls about seventy days later, on the day pilgrims at the hajj perform their sacrifice. Muslims everywhere who can afford it sacrifice a sheep, goat or cow, or pay for one to be sacrificed, and divide the meat in thirds: for the family, for friends and neighbors, and for the poor. The festival recalls the story, told in both the Qur'an and the Bible, of Abraham's readiness to offer his son; most Muslims understand the son to be Ishmael, while the Bible names Isaac. In the United States, families usually arrange the sacrifice through a farm or a charity that ships meat to those in need.

Both Eids show a pattern you will see across the tradition: a communal prayer, a required act of giving built into the holiday, and food shared beyond the family. Because the Islamic calendar is lunar, the Eids, like Ramadan, move through the seasons. Some school districts, including Chicago Public Schools, have begun listing the Eids on their calendars so that students can be absent without penalty, though practice varies from year to year.

words.d: an Islamic festival; the word means festival or feast
the festival of breaking the fast that ends Ramadan, marked by a morning prayer, giving and visiting
the festival of sacrifice held during the hajj, recalling Abraham's willingness to offer his son

look.title: Two Holidays, One Pattern
look.text: Eid al-Fitr: a donation before the prayer so the poor can celebrate, then prayer, then feasting. Eid al-Adha: prayer, then an animal sacrifice with a third of the meat given to the poor, then feasting. Compare this with a holiday you know from another tradition or from American civic life.
look.prompt: What does building a required gift into each festival say about how Islam ties worship to care for others? Does the holiday you chose do something similar?

check.q: What does Eid al-Fitr celebrate?
choices: The birth of Muhammad
The end of the hajj
The first revelation
The end of the Ramadan fast
check.why: Eid al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast, begins when Ramadan ends.

check.q: How is the meat from the Eid al-Adha sacrifice traditionally divided?

It is all given to the mosque
It is all eaten at the family feast
It is sold to pay for the hajj
check.why: The traditional division gives one third to the family, one third to friends and neighbors, and one third to those in need.

check.q: Which son do most Muslims believe Abraham prepared to sacrifice, and whom does the Bible name?
choices: Isaac in both traditions
Most Muslims say Ishmael; the Bible names Isaac
Most Muslims say Jacob; the Bible names Ishmael
Ishmael in both traditions
check.why: Most Muslim readers identify the son as Ishmael, while Genesis names Isaac; the shared story is read differently.

lessons.title: Inside a Mosque
lessons.mainIdea: A mosque is a place of prostration, arranged around the direction of Mecca, without images of God or people, and led in prayer by an imam.
reading: The Arabic word for mosque is *masjid*, a place of prostration, and the name tells you the building's main job: it is a clean, open space where people can line up and pray. Take off your shoes at the door, as everyone does, and you will see a carpeted hall with no pews. On the wall facing Mecca is a niche called the *mihrab*, which shows the qibla and helps carry the prayer leader's voice. Beside it stands the *minbar*, a set of steps from which the Friday sermon is given. Outside, many mosques have a tower, a minaret, from which the call to prayer was traditionally chanted.

You will not find statues or paintings of God, Muhammad or saints. Because of tawhid and the fear of shirk, images of living beings are traditionally avoided in places of worship. Instead, walls are decorated with Arabic calligraphy, often verses of the Qur'an or the names of God, and with geometric and floral patterns. A large mosque may have a dome, a courtyard, fountains for wudu, classrooms, a library and a kitchen. Men and women usually pray in separate areas or rows, in arrangements that vary from mosque to mosque.

The prayer leader is the *imam*, which simply means the one in front. In most Sunni communities the imam is not a priest with special powers; any knowledgeable adult can lead prayer, though larger mosques employ trained scholars who also teach, counsel and give the Friday sermon, the khutba. In Shia communities the title imam also has a deeper meaning, described in the next chapter. Islam has no central authority like a pope, and mosques are usually run by local boards.

The Chicago area has well over a hundred mosques, from converted storefronts to large purpose-built centers with domes and minarets in the southwest and northwest suburbs, and they serve communities whose families come from South Asia, the Arab world, Africa, Bosnia, Turkey and Iran, along with many African American and other American-born Muslims. Most welcome respectful visitors outside prayer times. Visitors are asked to dress modestly, remove shoes, and, for women in many mosques, cover their hair.

words.d: the Arabic word for mosque; it means a place of prostration
the niche in a mosque wall that marks the direction of Mecca
the stepped pulpit in a mosque from which the Friday sermon is given
the person who leads prayer in a mosque; in Shia Islam the term also names the Prophet's rightful successors

look.title: Reading a Building
look.text: Walk into a Catholic church and you see an altar at the front, a crucifix, stained glass with saints, and rows of pews facing forward. Walk into a mosque and you see an empty carpeted hall, a niche in one wall, a stepped pulpit, and calligraphy where the pictures would be.

The steps from which the sermon is given
The niche in the wall that marks the direction of Mecca
The fountain used for washing before prayer
check.why: The mihrab is the niche showing the qibla; the minbar is the pulpit and the minaret is the tower.

check.q: Why are images of God, Muhammad and people traditionally absent from mosques?
choices: Because paint was scarce in Arabia
Because the Qur'an forbids all art
Because only calligraphy is allowed in any Muslim building
Because of tawhid and the concern that images could lead to shirk
check.why: The teaching of God's oneness and the fear of worshiping anything besides God led to avoiding images of living beings in worship spaces.

choices: The person who leads prayer, not a priest with special powers
The head of all Muslims worldwide
A pilgrim who has completed the hajj
An angel who brings revelation

lessons.title: Halal: What Muslims Eat
lessons.mainIdea: Halal means permitted; Islamic food rules forbid pork, blood, alcohol and improperly slaughtered meat, and they shape shopping, cooking and eating out.
reading: Walk down Devon Avenue on Chicago's Far North Side and you pass grocery stores, butchers and restaurants with the word *halal* in their windows. Halal means permitted, and it applies to all of life, not only food; its opposite is *haram*, forbidden. For food, the Qur'an lists the main rules: Muslims do not eat pork or any pork product, blood, animals that died on their own, or animals sacrificed to anyone but God. They also do not drink wine or, by extension, any alcohol.

Meat from permitted animals such as chicken, lamb, goat and beef must be slaughtered in a prescribed way, called *zabiha* or dhabiha: by a Muslim, with a sharp knife across the throat, while pronouncing the name of God, and with the blood drained. Jewish kosher slaughter is similar, and the Qur'an says the food of the People of the Book is permitted to Muslims, so some Muslims will eat kosher meat when halal is not available; others will not. Seafood is generally considered halal, though schools of law differ on shellfish.

The rules reach into the details. Gelatin made from pork appears in some candies and marshmallows, and many Muslims check labels for it. Vanilla extract contains alcohol, and opinions differ on whether the tiny amount matters. Halal certification agencies now label products the way kosher agencies do, and Illinois passed a Halal Food Act in 2001 making it illegal to sell food falsely labeled as halal. Fast-food chains in Muslim neighborhoods often advertise halal meat.

As with fasting, the tradition builds in mercy. The Qur'an says that a person who eats forbidden food out of real necessity, without wanting to, is not at fault. And Muslims differ in practice: some eat only certified zabiha meat, some eat any meat except pork, some keep the rules strictly at home but loosely when traveling. A hospital or school cafeteria that serves Muslim students usually offers a vegetarian option, marks pork clearly, and, where possible, provides halal meat.

words.d: permitted under Islamic law; for food, what Muslims may eat
forbidden under Islamic law; for food, pork, blood, alcohol and improperly slaughtered meat
the prescribed Islamic method of slaughtering an animal, with God's name pronounced and the blood drained

look.title: A Cafeteria Serves Everyone
look.text: A hospital in Chicago serves patients who are Muslim, Jewish, Hindu, Christian and of no religion. The kitchen manager wants one menu that most patients can eat from without asking questions. She knows Jews who keep kosher avoid pork and shellfish and do not mix meat and milk, that many Hindus eat no beef and many are vegetarian, and that Muslims avoid pork and alcohol and prefer halal meat.

Permitted and forbidden
Clean and dirty
Meat and vegetables

Fish

Muhammad received the first revelation
Muhammad returned to Mecca and cleared the Kaaba of idols

choices: Detailed rules about inheritance
Short, urgent suras warning of judgment and calling to one God
Regulations for the community's treaties
Laws about marriage contracts

choices: Zakat: the pilgrimage to Mecca
Sawm: the declaration of faith
Salat: the five daily prayers
Hajj: fasting in Ramadan
review.why: Salat is ritual prayer; zakat is the yearly gift to the needy, sawm is fasting, and hajj is the pilgrimage.

Only the claim about Muhammad

choices: Why there are no images of God or people, only calligraphy and patterns
Why men and women sit together
Why shoes are worn inside
Why there are statues of the prophets
review.why: The teaching of God's absolute oneness and the concern about shirk led Muslims to avoid images of living beings in worship spaces.

choices: Muslims deny Jesus existed; Christians affirm he did
Both honor Jesus as born of Mary, but Muslims regard him as a prophet and Christians as the Son of God
Both traditions call him the final prophet

choices: Kosher food is always vegetarian
The Qur'an requires Muslims to eat Jewish food
Steakhouses serve only pork
Kosher slaughter is similar to zabiha and the Qur'an permits the food of the People of the Book, so some Muslims accept kosher meat
